tool.name: HabitatPatches
tool.summary: Turns a habitat suitability model into habitat PATCH polygons classified by whether each is large enough to matter: the HSM is averaged over a circular moving window, cells whose average meets your quality threshold become suitable habitat, touching suitable cells are grouped into patches, and each patch is classified by its GEODESIC area in hectares as too small, a breeding patch (supports at least one breeding event), or a population patch. One polygon per patch with class, name, and hectares, symbolized by class. A modernized port of the CorridorDesigner Patch Configuration tool. Needs no Spatial Analyst.
tool.usage:
WHY THIS TOOL EXISTS. A habitat model tells you how good each CELL is; it does not tell you whether the good cells represent an area large enough to support a species. The habitat patches answer that: contiguous suitable habitat is grouped into patches, and each patch is judged against two species-specific sizes from the workshop book -- the minimum area supporting at least one breeding event (a breeding patch) and the minimum area supporting a population (a population patch). Anything smaller is suitable ground that is functionally too small on its own.
HOW A CELL BECOMES A PATCH. First the HSM is AVERAGED over a circular moving window (the mean of the data cells -- the original tool's Focal Statistics MEAN with the DATA option), so a lone bad cell inside good habitat, or a lone good cell in bad habitat, does not fragment or fabricate patches; the window size is a species decision (the original species files ranged from a 3x3-cell rectangle for small animals to a 200 m circle for wide-ranging ones). Cells whose AVERAGE meets the habitat quality threshold count as suitable, suitable cells touching along edges OR corners join into one patch (the original's RegionGroup EIGHT), and each patch's area decides its class.
AREAS ARE GEODESIC HECTARES. The original counted pixels and multiplied by the nominal cell size, which silently assumed a meters projection (its own source code wonders about feet). This version sums each patch's TRUE per-row cell areas on the spheroid, so the hectare thresholds mean the same thing on any coordinate system, including geographic rasters and State Plane feet. The Area_Ha field holds the exact number the classification used.
READING THE OUTPUT. One polygon per patch: Class 1 / "Too small" (below the breeding size), Class 2 / "Breeding patch", Class 3 / "Population patch", each with its hectares. The layer arrives symbolized by class (dark green population, light green breeding, pale too-small; the legend labels the smallest class "Smaller than Breeding Patch"). The run messages report the patch count and total hectares per class, and warn if NO patch reaches the population size. The output carries the source model's analysis record forward, so the Corridor Analysis Data Report can describe the whole chain from factors to patches.
ENVIRONMENTS. This tool is grid-native: the analysis runs on the input raster' own grid, and the patch polygons are written in its coordinate system. The Output Coordinate System, Extent, Snap Raster, Cell Size, and Mask environment settings are deliberately NOT applied -- honoring them would move the analysis off the grid the hectare classification was computed on. To get the patches in another coordinate system, project the finished output with the Project tool as a deliberate step. The scratch workspace and overwrite-output settings are honored.
CREDITS AND REFERENCES. The original CorridorDesigner Patch Configuration tool is by Dan Majka (dan@corridordesign.org, 2006-2007); this ArcGIS Pro version is by Jeff Jenness and Dan Majka. Please cite: Majka, D., J. Jenness, and P. Beier. 2007. CorridorDesigner: ArcGIS tools for designing and evaluating corridors. http://corridordesign.org.

dialogReference.para: The habitat suitability model on the 0-100 scale (100 = best habitat) -- the product of the Create Habitat Suitability Model / Combine Habitat Factors / Modify HSM tools, or any model normalized onto that scale.

The radius of the circular window the HSM is averaged over before thresholding, so isolated cells do not fragment or fabricate patches. A species decision: the original species files used everything from a 3x3-cell rectangle (radius about 1 cell) for small animals to a 200 m circle for wide-ranging ones. On a geographic raster a linear-unit radius is sized per row on the spheroid.
Units of the moving-window radius: Cells, or a linear unit (Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles) converted to cells on the raster's own grid.
Cells whose WINDOW-AVERAGED suitability is at or above this value count as suitable habitat. The workshop book typically thresholds an HSM in the 50-60 range; it is a species judgment.

The smallest area of contiguous suitable habitat that supports at least one breeding event for this species, in hectares. Patches below this are classed "Too small"; patches at or above it are at least "Breeding patch".
The smallest area supporting a POPULATION of this species, in hectares -- at least the breeding size, usually several times larger. Patches at or above it are classed "Population patch".

The patch polygons: one feature per patch with PatchID, Class (1-3), Class_Name, and Area_Ha (the geodesic hectares the classification used). A name is suggested from the input model. The layer arrives symbolized by class.

scriptExample.title: Create Habitat Patches example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Patches for a model thresholded at 60, averaged over a 200 m window, with a 25 ha breeding patch and a 250 ha population patch.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
arcpy.jenness.HabitatPatches( r"C:\project\hsm\Bear_HSM.tif", 200, "Meters", 60, 25, 250, r"C:\project\hsm\Patches_Bear_HSM.shp")
